sections.html:
Central became a city on April 23, 2005, after residents voted to incorporate, so a house here answers to the City of Central rather than the Baton Rouge city-parish government. The effort grew out of a wish for a school system separate from East Baton Rouge Parish's. The Legislature allowed that only after incorporation, and residents are zoned to the Central Community School System. About 25,000 people lived here when the city formed.

Permits, planning and floodplain questions go to Central City Hall at 11530 Sullivan Road, phone 225.262.5000. The deed, however, is still recorded at the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court because Central sits inside that parish.

Central occupies the east-central part of East Baton Rouge Parish, between the Comite River on its west border and the Amite River, which forms the line with Livingston Parish. The two rivers meet near the southern edge of the city. It has 62.26 square miles of land, far more area than its population suggests.

Louisiana Highway 408 runs through the middle and leads about 7 miles west to Interstate 110 in north Baton Rouge, Louisiana Highway 37 crosses the east side, and downtown Baton Rouge is about 13 miles southwest. With a river on each side, where a house sits relative to the Comite and Amite is the first thing to understand about its flood history.

Central is overwhelmingly owner-occupied. The numbers below cover 2020 to 2024 for the whole city.

Housing measureCentral
Owner-occupied housing unit rate88.8%
Median value, owner-occupied homes$288,700
Median monthly owner costs with a mortgage$1,879
Median monthly owner costs without a mortgage$544
Median gross rent$1,309

The city has 11,496 households averaging 2.59 people. The population was 29,565 in 2020 and an estimated 30,313 on July 1, 2025.

Because so many homes are lived in by their owners, most sellers are homeowners rather than landlords. Common reasons to sell fast are a move, an inheritance, a divorce or repairs the owner cannot afford.

sections.h2: How did the 2016 flood affect Central?
sections.html:
Central was among the hardest-hit parts of East Baton Rouge Parish in August 2016, and the mayor put the number of affected residents at 25,000. The August 2016 flood far exceeded the flood of record in the Comite River basin, with about 109,000 homes flooded across Louisiana, 79,000 of them in East Baton Rouge and Livingston Parishes.

The Comite River Diversion is the project meant to reduce headwater flooding on this side of the parish. It involves a 12-mile channel and 23 contracts, all awarded by the end of fiscal year 2025, with six projects under construction.

Given that history, a buyer in Central will probably want to know:

  • Did this house take water in 2016, and how deep?
  • Was it gutted and rebuilt with permits?
  • Is there an elevation certificate on file?
  • Is the property in a regulatory floodway or a repetitive loss area?

The City of Central lets owners request a formal floodzone determination, and the result covers more than a zone letter. It can list the base flood elevation, a Community-Defined Flood Elevation, the FIRM panel number and effective date, and whether the property is in a regulatory floodway or a conveyance zone. It can also say whether the property is in a repetitive loss area and what the 2016 flood depth was at that spot. That last item replaces rumor with an official number when a buyer asks.

  • The city keeps elevation certificates on file for structures completed after 2008 and publishes a list of those properties.
  • An owner whose certificate shows the structure above the flood level may be able to seek removal from the floodplain through a Letter of Map Change.
  • Central takes part in the Community Rating System, which can lower flood insurance premiums.

Ordering the determination before you list answers a buyer's top question and hands the buyer's lender a document to work from.

Central requires permits for most work beyond cosmetic touch-ups: remodels, additions, roofing, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work, fences, generators and demolitions. Accessory buildings over 200 square feet and portable structures over 120 square feet also need one.

A separate disturbance permit applies before mechanized equipment disturbs land, trees are removed by machine, more than 12 cubic yards of soil, sand or fill is hauled in, or a structure is demolished with heavy equipment. The floodplain manager may approve up to 12 inches of fill without a geotechnical report. Deeper fill needs engineered lifts, a geotechnical report and a topography plan by a civil engineer, and it must not harm drainage on neighboring land. The Permit Desk is at 225.262.5000, extension 1.

If you raised a yard, added a carport or replaced a roof without a permit, an inspector or lender may flag it. Fixing that before an offer is easier than after. Ask the permit desk what it would take to close out or legalize past work, and keep any approval letters with your sale papers.

The Civil Code requires a sale of an immovable to be made by authentic act or by act under private signature. In practice you sign before a notary, and the act is recorded with the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court. The Recording Department's number is (225) 389-3985, and fees are due at recording. The 2026 mandatory forms, including the Property Disclosure, took effect on January 1, 2026.

Before closing, gather your deed, any elevation certificate or floodzone determination, repair invoices with permits, and mortgage payoff information. Your mortgage balance, taxes and recording fees come out of your proceeds at the table.

• Listing: Works for a repaired, dry house if you can wait for financing and an appraisal.
  • Selling as-is for cash: Fits a house with flood repairs, deferred work or a deadline.
  • Selling by owner: Saves the agent's role but leaves paperwork and buyer screening with you.

Ask any buyer for proof of funds or financing, and read cancellation terms before you sign.

Whichever route you pick, write down what you need to net after your mortgage payoff, taxes and closing costs. A seller who knows that number can compare a slower listing against a cash offer on a firm date without guessing. Central sellers with flood history should lead with the floodzone determination and permit records, since those documents answer the questions that otherwise slow negotiations.

faqs.q: Is Central part of Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: No. Central is its own city, incorporated on April 23, 2005, though it lies in East Baton Rouge Parish and the Baton Rouge metro area. It has its own city government and school system.

faqs.q: Which school system serves Central, LA?
faqs.a: The Central Community School System. Residents are zoned to it rather than to the parish system, because the Legislature allowed a separate system once the city incorporated.

faqs.q: How can I find out how deep the 2016 flood was at my Central house?
faqs.a: Request a floodzone determination from the City of Central. It can include the 2016 flood depth at the property, the base flood elevation, the FIRM panel and whether the property is in a floodway or repetitive loss area.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed for a house in Central?
faqs.a: At the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court, Recording Department, phone (225) 389-3985. Fees are due when the document is recorded.

faqs.q: What share of Central homes are owner-occupied?
faqs.a: 88.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, with a median owner-occupied home value of $288,700. These are citywide figures, not a value for any one house.
